summary: Stone tower east of Prescott, Ontario: a windmill fought over in 1838, lit as a St. Lawrence light in 1872, closed to visitors until June 2027.

lens.note: four mammoth flat-wick lamps with 16-inch reflectors, per the 1873 report

structures.note: 62 ft in the 1873 report; octagonal cast-iron lantern added at the conversion (register)

access.note: Battle of the Windmill National Historic Site (Parks Canada). Closed from September 2026 to May 2027 per the Parks Canada visitor page.

visit.note: LighthouseFriends (undated) says grounds open and tower open in season; site closed until June 2027 per Parks Canada.

events.note: About 1830 per LighthouseFriends (a windmill, built by Thomas Hughes). The station file's Parks Canada heritage data says 1833; that statement was not readable.
Hunters' invasion; battle at the windmill, 12 to 16 November 1838; Hunter leaders chose Prescott in the fall of 1838
Milling operations ceased permanently after the battle; British troops occupied the tower for a year
Converted to a lighthouse in 1872 (register). The 1873 report says first exhibited on 15 June 'last', which read as June 1872 agrees.
Bernard Kean appointed 31 May 'last' at $150 a year (1873 report, as quoted by LighthouseFriends)
Ward Skinner Plumb's appointment cancelled on the minister's recommendation; John Fraser made keeper (LighthouseFriends)
National historic site designation, per LighthouseFriends. The register gives 1923.
Designated a national historic site of Canada (register)
Declared a Classified Federal Heritage Building
Friends of Windmill Point opened the lighthouse to the public
Designated a heritage lighthouse by the federal government
Lighthouse closed for roof repairs; $373,000 federal grant
Site closed from September 2026 to May 2027 (Parks Canada)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The register gives 1872 for the conversion. The 1873 report says the light was first exhibited on 15 June 'last'; read as June 1872, that agrees with the register. The station file's 1873 is not supported by either source.
LighthouseFriends dates the national historic site designation 1920; the register dates the national historic site of Canada designation 1923. Both are kept in the story.

notes_for_editor: Fact-checked 2026-10-27. Corrections made: (a) the Herald's Prescott postmaster letter does not mention the stone mill; that phrase is from a Courier and Enquirer correspondent writing from the steamer Telegraph on 14 November, now attributed correctly; (b) the 'stone mill' letter and the 'all killed or taken prisoners' note are now attributed separately (a note on the back of a proclamation from J. Ward Birge, not the same sheet as the Phenix); (c) the Hunters' choice of Prescott is dated to the fall of 1838, not November; (d) the opening's 1872 or 1873 is now 1872, and the 'sources differ on the year' claim is replaced by the June 1872 reading of the 1873 report; (e) the Phenix reprints a Sackett's Harbor Journal extra, now stated; (f) the Trowbridge and postmaster counts (100 to 150) are added beside LighthouseFriends' 250 and the Phenix's 500. Open points: (1) build date: station file 1833; LighthouseFriends about 1830; register gives no date; unresolved. (2) National historic site date 1920 (LighthouseFriends) vs 1923 (register); both kept. (3) The Phenix masthead, read by OCR, says NOV. 21 but the loc.gov date and the Saturday weekday are 24 November; the 24 November date is kept. (4) The 1873 Marine report is not in the local corpus; the 31 May and 15 June dates rest on LighthouseFriends' quotation. (5) Keeper tables in the 1900 to 1910 corpus volumes were not matched by position for this station. (6) The 1922, 1928, 1989, 2013 and 2015 facts rest on LighthouseFriends alone. (7) Newspaper quotations are from OCR text read with newspapers.py --page; OCR errors kept.
